I tried using it on a fairly weird model of mine.
The data are dichotomous responses assumed to be generated from a 2PL model.
However, the purpose of the model is not to just estimate a 2PL IRT model, but to detect latent groups which some items exhibit DIF between.
So it's a fairly convoluted model --- The likelihood for each item and case is a mixture of bernoulli likelihoods, one which assumes DIF one which does not; when it assumes DIF, it is another mixture model aiming to assign individuals to latent clusters.
Moreover, one can 'predict' latent cluster membership using softmax or logistic regression from other respondent data.

Needless to say, ADVI did not work well. Optimizing doesn't either, presumably because this sort of problem needs an EM approach, not a basic ML approach.

I wanted to try ADVI because the model takes about 1200 seconds for 300 cases and 24 items.
I did try the fullrank, it didn't work well either.

By 'didnt work well', I mean it completely fails to estimate the correct latent group memberships (which I know, because I generate the data) and fails to discern the DIF items from non-DIF items.

messages.subject: Re: advi feedback from users
parts:
I have tried ADVI lately on three different kinds of models:

- Small negative binomial regressions, just out of curiosity. Full rank, didn't always estimate the theta parameter well. Not many replications to estimate it, so I'm not surprised ADVI has problems. 

- A simple non-negative regression model with fairly big count data (~ 100000, seven covariates), where I needed only point estimates for a recommender system. Full rank, works as expected. 

- A nonnegative component model for count data, with some hierarchy in the model. 240k counts, 10k parameters. Mean field, works well and is surprisingly fast with the new indexing notation (4 minutes). Our goal is not to make exact inference, but to find descriptive components. Goes to local minima etc., but this is not ADVI's fault. Sometimes throws an overflow, don't remember which function it comes from. 

A colleague has tested mean-field ADVI for a Poisson Factorisation model, with about 3M lines of data and at least the same number of parameters. (log-)Gaussian may not fit well with the posterior, or maybe the default gamma parametrisation was bad for mean field. 

All these are quick tests made in the context of commercial projects or theses, so we don't have definite reports or papers to show.

Is the reason NUTS is having a hard time due to run time and
scaling?

The model (below) is similar to the PPCA model in the ADVI paper. So some of the reasons why ADVI worked well for those models sort of applies here. Stan fits it with NUTS pretty quickly actually. The problem is that N_eff is low for some of the variables, like 3 for mu_F and 10 for lp__ out of 1000 in my last run (also rhat is above 2 for mu_F and above 1.2 for lp__). One of the best things I did when I was just playing around with NUTS was constraining B to be a unit_vector. I think this is because it helps lock down what B is in some sort of range and helps F get identified.

data {
    //sizes
    int<lower=1> T;
    int<lower=1> N;
   
    //data
    matrix[T, N] Y;
}
transformed data {
    real<lower=0> one_over_sqrt_N;
   
    one_over_sqrt_N = 1 / sqrt(N);
}
parameters {
    real mu_F;
    real<lower=0> sd_F;
    vector[T] F;
    real<lower=0> sd_B;
    unit_vector[N] B;

    real<lower=0> sd_e;
}
model {
    mu_F ~ normal(0, 0.25);
    sd_F ~ normal(0, 6);
    F ~ normal(mu_F, sd_F);
    sd_B ~ normal(0, one_over_sqrt_N);
    B ~ normal(0, sd_B);

    to_vector(Y) ~ normal(to_vector(F * B'), sd_e);

}

I have finally got to something that fits my data with reasonable N_eff using NUTS (300 of 1000 for lp__, 1000 of 1000 for all hyperparameters, rhats between 1 and 1.01) and thought I would share (below). ADVI also fits it reasonably well. Of the hyperparameters, sd_z was higher than NUTS and the standard deviations of mu_z and sd_z were bigger than NUTS. But overall, it looks like it fits it well.

As many folks have noted, identification is very important for these PPCA-like models. What I really needed was a way to constrain w to be a positive unit normal vector. This isn't in Stan. However, I was able to make a close enough approximation by noting that var(w) should equal 1/N - mean(w)^2 for all unit vectors. The approach I took below uses this formula to constrain the mean. Since I didn't mind that w>0, it worked out pretty well. I also put a reasonably strong prior on the standard deviation of w, combined with constraints so mean(w) didn't have any imaginary variables in it.

Another thing I tried was to constrain z to have mean of 0 AND standard deviation of 1. The Stan documentation does a good job explaining how to force mean of 0, but it's harder than you would think to also force standard deviation of 1 while having the whole thing be identified properly (The only way I was able to do it resulted in lp__ near zero because the raw z values were not identified. The approach usually fit the data well, but it can be hard to diagnose problems when you're not printing all the variables). I tried holding back a second data point and did the math so that it works out, but it's very easy to get imaginary terms that screw it all up. So I gave up on that.

I would really love if Stan had better support for these kinds of constraints. Positive unit vectors seems do-able, but I don't know about forced unit normals.

data {
    int<lower=0> T;
    int<lower=0> N;
    vector[T] x[N];
}
transformed data {
    real<lower=0> one_over_N;
    real<lower=0> one_over_square_root_N;
    real<lower=0> sd_w_prior;
   
    one_over_N = 1.0 / N;
    one_over_square_root_N = sqrt(one_over_N);
    sd_w_prior = 1 / (sqrt(2 * N) * inv_Phi(0.95)); //selected so 95% of
                                                    //distribution is below
                                                    //(1 / sqrt(N))
}
parameters {
    real mu_z;
    real<lower=0> sd_z;
    vector[T] z;
    real<lower=0, upper=one_over_square_root_N> sd_w;
    vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] w;
    real<lower=0> sd_e;
}
transformed parameters {
    real<lower=0, upper=one_over_square_root_N> mu_w;

    mu_w = sqrt(one_over_N - square(sd_w));
}
model {
    mu_z ~ normal(0, 0.5);
    sd_z ~ normal(1, 0.5);
    z ~ normal(mu_z, sd_z);
    sd_w ~ normal(0, sd_w_prior);
    w ~ normal(mu_w, sd_w);
    sd_e ~ normal(0, 0.05);
   
    for (n in 1:N)
        x[n] ~ normal(z * w[n], sd_e);

}

Thanks for reporting back. That's great to know that it lines
up pretty closely in your application.

Did you try non-centered parameterizations of z and w? Not
sure if it'd be better or worse.

We have a unit vector type. If you declare

unit_vector[K] x;

it ensures x' * x = 1 and the default distribution is uniform
over all unit vectors.

The way it does it is as if we'd written it out by hand like this:

parameters {
vector[K] x_raw;

transformed parameters {
vector[K] x = x / dot_self(x);

model {
x_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

This ensures that the distribution on x is uniform over
the unit vectors. See:

Marsaglia, G. (1972). Choosing a point from the surface of a sphere.
The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 43(2):645–646.

I'm not sure about a fully standardized type. You might be
able to construct it the way we construct the unit vector.

When I was using those x_raws, I would get into a habit of ignoring the lp__, so other things could be going wrong in the model and I wouldn't realize it until much later. The only thing I could think of is if the calculation of N_eff for lp__ understands to ignore transformed variables that are not part of the final model.

Also, I was very familiar with unit_vector. My point is that you can't say
unit_vector<lower=0>[N] w;
or some sort of
positive_unit_vector[N] w;

What I did in the model was enforce an approximate unit vector that was always positive (I don't think I can get it exact with this approach because I get imaginary numbers). The reason I included it is that the sign of z and the sign of w weren't identified in any way. Sometimes the model would output w>0 and some z[i] > 0 and sometimes it would output w<0 with that z[i] <0. Forcing w > 0 helped keep it identified in a way that putting priors on the mean of z could not. I got much better results when I included this constraint vs. doing the analysis with just the unit_vector. Indeed, the problem of nailing down the sign seems similar to the issue discussed in the Stan manual under "Inference under Label Switching" in the "Finite Mixtures" section. Unlike finite mixtures, you may not have the information necessary to put a prior that enforces the constraint in a more general PPCA model.

A more general approach would probably to be something like below. This ensures that the largest square value is always positive. I haven't tried it yet and I don't know how well Stan would handle it, but I think it would be more useful than the positive_unit_vector above since it would allow sign identification in all these PPCA models, not just my specific case where I know all the w's are positive.

parameters {

}
transformed parameters {
     unit_vector[N] w;

     w = raw_w;

}

Anything that helps identify these models would be helpful.

One thing that I found very helpful was sampling from a simplified model a number of times and plotting pairs of statistics from them.

I'm attaching an R script that simulates from just the factor component of a 1-dimensional PPCA model. I included three charts that illustrate the three main ways that correlations can impact the model:
1) The deterministic relationship between the standard deviation and mean that is caused by taking the norm. This is the only thing I was correcting for in the code above.
2) There is an inverse relationship between the standard deviation of W and Z. This is likely because there is a limit on the variance of WZ and a higher value of the variance of W means a lower value for the variance of Z. The standard deviation of the standard deviation of Z also increases in the inverse of the standard deviation of W.
3) There is a positive relationship between the standard deviation of Z and the standard deviation of the mean of Z. This chart doesn't show it, but there is also a positive relationship between the standard deviation of Z and the mean of Z, but it only becomes apparent if the mean of Z is bigger than zero.

Also, it's amazing how different the charts looks when you change the variables. For instance, if you make the standard on the mu_W_sim equal to 0.1 instead of 1, then there is no correlation between sd_Z_norm and mu_Z_norm. The correlation between sd_W_norm and sd_Z_norm is still there, but much less pronounced. Thus, I suspect the fact that the reason I had better results with the unit vector constrained to be positive was because it kept the standard deviation of W in such a range that it kept these correlations from widening out too much.
On Friday, February 17, 2017 at 8:30:06 PM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:

Actually, positive_unit_vector is _much_ easier to implement 
than unit_vector as the half sphere is isomorphic to R^{n}.  Not
sure if there’s enough use cases to warrant the work to include
it in Stan, though.  Maybe a useful intro project for new devs.
On Feb 17, 2017, at 7:50 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:

+1 on the standardize function!

In the early iterations I had tried non-centered parameterization for these, but not in the most recent version of the model. I have sufficient data so that there isn't much pooling going on. I calculate a lambda score using a formula in Gelman's book and it is near zero after fitting the model (I noticed that non-centered parameterization helps most when lambda is above 0.5, indicating lots of pooling). 

On unit_normal and standardizing: the issue with the way you present them is that the x_raw's don't get identified. As a result, the N_eff's will be near zero for those, which is not a big deal, but it is a big deal for lp__. I really like being able to use lp__ as a diagnostic. I don't typically print all the variables to the screen, just the hyperparamters and lp__. If lp__ is near zero, then at that point I would inspect what's going on with the other variables, If not, then I assume they are fine. When I was using those x_raws, I would get into a habit of ignoring the lp__, so other things could be going wrong in the model and I wouldn't realize it until much later. The only thing I could think of is if the calculation of N_eff for lp__ understands to ignore transformed variables that are not part of the final model. 

Also, I was very familiar with unit_vector. My point is that you can't say 
unit_vector<lower=0>[N] w;
or some sort of 
positive_unit_vector[N] w;

What I did in the model was enforce an approximate unit vector that was always positive (I don't think I can get it exact with this approach because I get imaginary numbers). The reason I included it is that the sign of z and the sign of w weren't identified in any way. Sometimes the model would output w>0 and some z[i] > 0 and sometimes it would output w<0 with that z[i] <0. Forcing w > 0 helped keep it identified in a way that putting priors on the mean of z could not. I got much better results when I included this constraint vs. doing the analysis with just the unit_vector. Indeed, the problem of nailing down the sign seems similar to the issue discussed in the Stan manual under "Inference under Label Switching" in the "Finite Mixtures" section. Unlike finite mixtures, you may not have the information necessary to put a prior that enforces the constraint in a more general PPCA model. 

A more general approach would probably to be something like below. This ensures that the largest square value is always positive. I haven't tried it yet and I don't know how well Stan would handle it, but I think it would be more useful than the positive_unit_vector above since it would allow sign identification in all these PPCA models, not just my specific case where I know all the w's are positive. 

parameters {
     unit_vector[N] raw_w;
}
transformed parameters {
     unit_vector[N] w;

     w = raw_w;
     if (abs(max(w)) < abs(min(w)))
          w = -w;
}
On Fri, Feb 17, 2017 at 6:09 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

Thanks for reporting back.  That's great to know that it lines
up pretty closely in your application.

Did you try non-centered parameterizations of z and w?  Not
sure if it'd be better or worse.

We have a unit vector type.  If you declare

  unit_vector[K] x;

it ensures x' * x = 1 and the default distribution is uniform
over all unit vectors.

The way it does it is as if we'd written it out by hand like this:

parameters {
  vector[K] x_raw;

transformed parameters {
  vector[K] x = x / dot_self(x);

model {
  x_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

This ensures that the distribution on x is uniform over
the unit vectors.  See:

Marsaglia, G. (1972). Choosing a point from the surface of a sphere.
The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 43(2):645–646.

I'm not sure about a fully standardized type.  You might be
able to construct it the way we construct the unit vector.
The transform is just:

  vector[K] x = (x - mean(x)) / sd(x);

but it's not going to identify on the original y scale.  We
really need a function standardize(x) to replace that RHS with
efficient analytic derivatives.

- Bob

parameters {
simplex[K] y_raw;

vector<lower=0>[K] y = sqrt(y_raw);

You have to take the Jacobian into account if you want to put
a distribution on y, but that's trivial for sqrt(), being
just |sqrt'(x)|, so on the log scale in Stan dropping constants
and vectorizing, it's just

target += -log(sum(y));

though you should check my work on that.

I was able to get a one-dimensional PPCA working pretty well in some other constrained circumstances that would be applicable to some of my problems, but never was able to get it work (in the sense of having large N_eff for all variables and lp__) in a more general case that would work with any PPCA. Often, I would get a version working, then multiply the distribution by -1, re-run it, and get gibberish results.

One of my takeaways is the connection of PPCA to finite mixtures: any {w, z} will be equivalent to {-w, -z}. This will cause the mean of z to have a bimodal symmetric distribution a lot of the time. Sometimes also with the mean of w, depending on the assumptions. It can get pretty tricky.
